members.dotPoint: conduct practical investigations to measure temperature changes in examples of endothermic and exothermic reactions, including:
members.title: Hot or cold: endothermic and exothermic
members.exam: A common slip is calling the cold water the reaction, or saying an endothermic change "gives out cold". Marks go to naming the water as the surroundings, linking a temperature fall to heat absorbed (ΔH positive) and a rise to heat released (ΔH negative), and using the mass of water, not of solid or fuel, in q = mcΔT.
members.summary: A can of water over a spirit burner, or a cup of water with an ionic solid dissolving in it, sits beside an enthalpy level diagram. Drag the slider to react more substance: heat arrows flow out of or into the chemicals, the thermometer in the water climbs or drops, and the gap between the reactant and product levels grows.

members.dotPoint: use modelling to illustrate entropy changes in reactions
members.title: Predicting entropy change from an equation
members.exam: A common slip is counting every mole in the equation instead of only the gas moles, or ignoring state symbols. A full answer states the gas moles on each side (for example 4 mol to 2 mol of gas), then gives the sign: fewer gas particles, entropy decreases, ΔS < 0.
members.summary: A closed container of particles for six balanced equations. Raise the reaction progress and reactant particles turn into products, so you can watch gas particles appear or vanish and read off whether entropy increases or decreases.

cells.bigIdea: Every reaction is a start, a finish and a hill in between. The energy change depends only on start and finish, which is why Hess's Law works and a catalyst can't touch it. The hill is all route: it sets how hard a reaction is to get going, not where it ends up.

members.dotPoint: conduct practical investigations to observe and measure the quantitative relationships of chemical reactions, including but not limited to:
members.title: Conservation of mass in a reaction
members.exam: The common slip is writing that mass is "lost" or "used up" when a gas fizzes off. Marks go to saying a gas left an open system, that the mass drop equals the mass of gas produced, and to checking that mass against the gas volume using moles.
members.summary: Marble chips react with hydrochloric acid in a flask on a balance. In a stoppered, sealed flask the reading holds at 151.00 g while the CO₂ stays trapped; in an open beaker the reading falls by the mass of carbon dioxide that escapes, and a graph tracks both.

members.dotPoint: relate stoichiometry to the law of conservation of mass in chemical reactions by investigating:
members.title: Balancing equations atom by atom
members.exam: The classic slip is changing a subscript (writing H₂O₂ to fix the oxygen) instead of a coefficient, or not recounting every element after each change. Marks come from a fully balanced equation in lowest whole numbers, then using its mole ratio, not the mass ratio, in mass calculations.
members.summary: Pick a reaction and set the coefficients: reactant molecules break apart and their atoms slide across to build the products. Spare atoms glow on the left and empty slots show on the right until every element balances, while tally bars compare atom counts or total masses on each side.

members.dotPoint: conduct practical investigations to determine the concentrations of solutions and investigate the different ways in which concentrations are measured (ACSCH046, ACSCH063)
members.title: Concentration and dilution
members.exam: The usual slips are using the volume of water added as V₂, and leaving V in mL inside c = n ÷ V. Marks go to stating that dilution leaves the moles of solute unchanged, writing c₁V₁ = c₂V₂ with V₂ as the final solution volume, and converting mL to L before using c = n ÷ V.
members.summary: Fifty copper(II) and sulfate ion dots sit in a container of solution. Drag the volume slider and the liquid rises, the same dots spread out and the colour fades, while a graph of c against V shows the concentration falling along a curve whose rectangle c × V never changes area.

members.dotPoint: conduct a practical investigation to demonstrate and calculate the molar mass (mass of one mole) of:
members.title: Molar Mass
members.exam: Students lose marks by forgetting to multiply everything in a bracket or the water in a hydrate, by mixing up mass and moles in a limiting reagent question, and by dropping units. Show M as a sum, write n = m/M with numbers substituted, and give g/mol and mol.
members.summary: Pick a substance and a bar builds its molar mass from its atoms, with each element's percentage by mass beneath. Raise the sample mass and mole buckets fill, one bucket per mole, while moles and particle count update.

cells.subject: Chemistry

members.dotPoint: explore homogeneous mixtures and heterogeneous mixtures through practical investigations:
members.title: Separating mixtures by physical properties
members.exam: A common slip is naming a technique without the property it relies on, or dividing by the wrong mass. Marks come from pairing each step with its property (filtration: particle size, after dissolving the salt) and dividing each component's dry mass by the original sample mass, then checking the percentages sum to about 100%.
members.summary: A beaker of sand, salt and iron filings is run through three stations (a magnet, a filter funnel and an evaporating basin) and each component lands in its own dish, labelled with its recovered mass and its percentage of the original sample.

members.dotPoint: classify the elements based on their properties and position in the periodic table through their:
members.title: Trends across the periodic table
members.exam: The common slip is stating a trend with no reason. The mark goes to the chain: name what changes (core charge across a period, number of shells and shielding down a group), link it to the outer electrons' distance from the nucleus, then to the property. Know the ionisation energy dips at groups 13 and 16 too.
members.summary: A main-group periodic table (periods 1 to 6) recoloured by atomic radius, first ionisation energy, electronegativity, state at 25 °C or reactivity with water, with a slider that steps through the elements and a bar chart of the trend across the selected period or down its group.

members.dotPoint: investigate energy levels in atoms and ions through:
members.title: Flame colours and electron energy levels
members.exam: Students often say the heat itself makes the colour, or that light is given out when the electron absorbs energy. Marks go to the full sequence: energy absorbed, electron promoted to a higher level, electron falls back, photon emitted with energy equal to the gap (ΔE = hf), so each metal has its own colour.
members.summary: A metal ion sits in a flame. Tap a metal or drag the energy gap and watch its electron jump up an energy ladder, fall back, and fire a photon that lights one line on the emission spectrum and tints the flame. Toggle between Bohr orbits and Schrödinger orbital clouds.

members.dotPoint: investigate the properties of unstable isotopes using natural and human-made radioisotopes as examples, including but not limited to:
members.title: Alpha, beta and gamma decay
members.exam: Students often balance only the mass numbers, write a beta particle as ⁰₁e, or forget to change the element symbol. Marks come from showing A and Z both balancing, writing β− as ⁰₋₁e and β+ as ⁰₊₁e, and naming the daughter from its new atomic number.
members.summary: A nucleus fires an alpha particle, a beta-minus electron, a beta-plus positron or a gamma photon at paper, aluminium and lead. The nuclear equation above it fills in the daughter element as the mass and atomic numbers balance, and each emission stops where its penetrating power runs out.

members.dotPoint: investigate the role of electronegativity in determining the ionic or covalent nature of bonds between atoms
members.title: Ionic versus covalent bonding
members.exam: Students often call any bond with different atoms ionic, or say ionic means sharing. Marks come from quoting the electronegativity difference, naming the bond as non-polar, polar or ionic, and backing it with positions on the periodic table. In Lewis diagrams for ionic compounds, show brackets and charges, not shared pairs.
members.summary: Two atoms sit side by side while an electronegativity-difference slider drags their bonding electron pair from evenly shared, to lopsided with δ+ and δ− charges, to fully handed over as ions. The Lewis dot diagram and the two elements’ places on a mini periodic table update alongside.

members.dotPoint: investigate elements that possess the physical property of allotropy
members.title: Allotropes of carbon
members.exam: A common slip is saying graphite conducts because of electrons "between the layers", or that its layers are held by covalent bonds. The mark comes from linking structure to property: three covalent bonds per carbon leave one delocalised electron that moves along each layer, and weak dispersion forces between layers let them slide.
members.summary: Pick an allotrope of carbon and push the top of it sideways: diamond's 3D network only strains, graphite's layers slide apart, a graphene sheet ripples without breaking, and buckyballs roll over each other.

members.dotPoint: investigate the different chemical structures of atoms and elements, including but not limited to:
members.title: Ionic, covalent and metallic structures
members.exam: The classic slip: saying melting iodine or ice breaks covalent bonds. It only overcomes weak forces between molecules. Marks come from naming the particles, the force that must be overcome, and linking that to the property, e.g. ions fixed in a solid lattice cannot carry charge.
members.summary: Four lattices side by side (ionic network, covalent network, covalent molecular and metallic) that you heat, strike or wire into a circuit, so melting point, brittleness and conductivity visibly fall out of each structure.

members.dotPoint: explore the similarities and differences between the nature of intermolecular and intramolecular bonds and the strength of the forces associated with each, in order to explain the:
members.title: Bonds within versus forces between
members.exam: The classic slip is writing that boiling water breaks O–H bonds or breaks the bonds in the molecule. Marks come from naming the specific intermolecular force overcome (dispersion, dipole–dipole or hydrogen bonding), stating the covalent bonds within stay intact, and saying network and ionic solids melt high because strong bonds must break.
members.summary: Particles of chlorine, water, silicon or sodium chloride heat up on a temperature slider: solid lines are bonds within, dashed lines are forces between, and two bars compare the energy to break each. Molecular substances lose only the dashed lines when they melt and boil; silicon and salt must break their solid lines.

members.dotPoint: investigate the basic structure of stable and unstable isotopes by examining:
members.title: Protons, neutrons and isotopes
members.exam: The common slip is averaging the isotope masses without weighting them, or forgetting to divide the weighted sum by 100. Marks come from multiplying each relative isotopic mass by its percentage abundance, adding, dividing by 100, and giving Ar with no units. In notation, A sits top-left and Z bottom-left, and neutrons = A − Z.
members.summary: A nucleus you can build: pick an element, add or remove neutrons and watch the nuclide symbol, mass number and stability change while the protons and electrons stay put. Beside it, a mass spectrum turns isotope abundances into the weighted relative atomic mass, or flips to the band of stable nuclei.

members.dotPoint: model the atom’s discrete energy levels, including electronic configuration and spdf notation (ACSCH017, ACSCH018, ACSCH020, ACSCH022)
members.title: Electron shells filling up
members.exam: Common slips: filling 3d before 4s, putting three electrons in one orbital, superscripts that do not add up to the atomic number, and writing calcium as 2,8,10 instead of 2,8,8,2. Marks come from the correct filling order, counts that match Z, and knowing the Cr and Cu exceptions.
members.summary: An energy ladder of s, p and d orbital boxes fills one electron at a time as the slider raises the atomic number, writing the spdf configuration underneath; a toggle swaps the same electrons onto Bohr shells with 2n² capacity bars.

cells.subject: Physics

members.dotPoint: Explain the role of the movement of electrons in charging particles and objects
members.title: Charging by friction, conduction and induction
members.exam: The usual slip is saying protons or positive charge moved. In solids only electrons transfer, so write "the wool lost electrons", never "the rod gained positive charge". For induction, give the order (earth, break the earth, then remove the rod) and state the object ends with the opposite sign to the rod; by conduction it gets the same sign.
members.summary: Four benches of static: rub polythene on wool, touch a charged metal sphere to a neutral one, bring a charged rod near an earthed sphere, and build a thundercloud over the ground. The amber + signs are fixed proton charges and the glowing dots are electrons, which travel as you step through each method while the net charge readout updates.

members.dotPoint: Solve problems involving changes in electric potential energy in a uniform electric field using W=qV=qEd and W=ΔKE
members.title: A charge speeding up between charged plates
members.exam: A common slip is using the full plate separation d when the charge has only crossed part of the gap, or forgetting to convert centimetres to metres. Use W = qEx for the distance actually travelled, W = qV for the whole gap, set W = ΔK to find speed, and state that potential energy falls as kinetic energy rises.
members.summary: A proton or an electron released from rest between two charged plates. Set the voltage, the plate separation and how far the charge has travelled, and watch the work done by the field drain the potential energy bar into the kinetic energy bar, with W = qEx worked out underneath.

members.dotPoint: Analyse the relationships between voltage, potential energy difference and work when changing the position of a charge in a uniform electric field using V=ΔUq
members.title: Voltage as energy per charge
members.exam: Students mix up voltage and energy, writing that a bigger charge has a bigger voltage. Voltage is energy per coulomb, so q changes ΔU, not ΔV. Marks come from writing W = ΔU = qΔV with units (J, C, V), using ΔV = Ed only in a uniform field, and stating the sign: positive charge gains energy moving towards higher potential.
members.summary: A positive charge is pushed from the 0 V plate towards the 120 V plate across a uniform field. A blue column shows the energy per microcoulomb (the voltage), a gold column stacks the total energy ΔU = qΔV, and tripling the charge triples the gold column while the blue one stays put.

members.dotPoint: Calculate electric current using I=qt
members.title: Current as flowing charge
members.exam: Students often draw conventional current the way the electrons move, or plug minutes and microcoulombs straight into I = q/t. Draw the arrow from + to − outside the cell, convert to coulombs and seconds first (2 min = 120 s), and give the answer in amperes.
members.summary: Free electrons drift through a metal wire between two terminals and a dashed gate counts the charge crossing it each second, which equals the current; the conventional current arrow points the other way, and switching to AC makes the drift and both arrows swing back and forth.

members.dotPoint: Relate voltage to electron flow in a circuit of constant resistance
members.title: Ohm's law and resistance
members.exam: Students often call the gradient of an I–V graph the resistance. With I on the vertical axis the gradient is 1/R, and for a non-ohmic device R = V/I at that point, not the tangent slope. Put the ammeter in series and the voltmeter in parallel, and say a metal wire is ohmic only at constant temperature.
members.summary: Electrons drift through a lattice of vibrating ions in a wire wired to a cell, while the I–V graph traces out as you raise the voltage. Change the material, length, diameter or temperature and the straight line tilts; switch to a filament globe and the line bends into a curve.

members.dotPoint: Relate power to energy transformations
members.title: Electrical power and energy in circuits
members.exam: Students often treat voltage as energy rather than energy per coulomb, or forget to convert minutes to seconds in ΔE = PΔt. Write the chain I = Q/t, V = E/Q, P = VI = ΔE/Δt, keep SI units (J, C, s, W), and name what the energy becomes (light, heat) when asked about transformations.
members.summary: Charges circle a battery-and-globe loop carrying gold energy halos that shrink to nothing in the globe; dragging the voltage makes the halos bigger, the charges faster, the globe brighter and the P = VI rectangle grow in both directions at once.

members.dotPoint: Compare the connection of components in series circuits with that in parallel circuits
members.title: Series and parallel circuits
members.exam: Common slips: putting a voltmeter in series, saying current is used up by the first resistor, or forgetting to flip 1/R at the end. Marks come from showing the same current at every point in series, voltages that add to the supply, branch currents that add in parallel, and a parallel total below the smallest branch. In practical reports, explain measured-versus-calculated gaps with named causes.
members.summary: A live circuit schematic with a 12 V battery, resistors, ammeters in series and voltmeters across each resistor. Switch between series, parallel and combination circuits, drag R₂, and the moving charge speeds up, slows or splits while every meter reads the new value.

members.dotPoint: Identify that magnetic field lines are continuous and used to represent the strength and direction of magnetic fields
members.title: Reading magnetic field lines
members.exam: Common slips: lines that stop at the S pole or start in mid-air, lines that cross, or no arrows. To earn the marks, draw closed loops with arrows from N to S outside (and S to N inside if shown), never let lines cross, and draw them closer together near the poles.
members.summary: A bar magnet with its field lines drawn as closed loops that run through the magnet. A compass slides along a track, its needle turning to follow the gold line through it, while a bracket shows the gap to the next line widening as the field weakens; a toggle swaps to an N pole facing an S pole with a uniform field in the gap.

members.dotPoint: Calculate the strength of the uniform magnetic field inside a solenoid using B=μ0NIL
members.title: What makes an electromagnet stronger
members.exam: A common slip is leaving L in centimetres, or thinking a longer coil with the same turns is stronger. In a test, convert L to metres, write B = μ₀NI/L with the substitution shown and give the unit, tesla. In a practical report, name the one variable you changed and the ones you kept constant.
members.summary: A side view of a solenoid whose turns, current, length and core you can change. The field lines inside get closer together as B = μ₀NI/L grows, and a working line calculates B from the values on screen.

pick.dotPoint: Explain the role of the movement of electrons in charging particles and objects
pick.title: Charging by friction, conduction and induction
pick.exam: The usual slip is saying protons or positive charge moved. In solids only electrons transfer, so write "the wool lost electrons", never "the rod gained positive charge". For induction, give the order (earth, break the earth, then remove the rod) and state the object ends with the opposite sign to the rod; by conduction it gets the same sign.
pick.summary: Four benches of static: rub polythene on wool, touch a charged metal sphere to a neutral one, bring a charged rod near an earthed sphere, and build a thundercloud over the ground. The amber + signs are fixed proton charges and the glowing dots are electrons, which travel as you step through each method while the net charge readout updates.

runnersUp.dotPoint: Solve problems involving changes in electric potential energy in a uniform electric field using W=qV=qEd and W=ΔKE
runnersUp.title: A charge speeding up between charged plates
runnersUp.exam: A common slip is using the full plate separation d when the charge has only crossed part of the gap, or forgetting to convert centimetres to metres. runnersUp.summary: A proton or an electron released from rest between two charged plates. Set the voltage, the plate separation and how far the charge has travelled, and watch the work done by the field drain the potential energy bar into the kinetic energy bar, with W = qEx worked out underneath.

runnersUp.dotPoint: Analyse the relationships between voltage, potential energy difference and work when changing the position of a charge in a uniform electric field using V=ΔUq
runnersUp.title: Voltage as energy per charge

runnersUp.summary: A positive charge is pushed from the 0 V plate towards the 120 V plate across a uniform field. runnersUp.dotPoint: Calculate electric current using I=qt

members.dotPoint: Derive a=gsinθ-μgcosθ to describe the acceleration on an object on an inclined plane with friction using Newton’s second law parallel to the plane

members.dotPoint: Describe examples of the law of reflection

members.exam: The classic slip is measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal, or swapping n₁ and n₂. Show the substitution and units when using v = c/n.
members.summary: A light beam, with its wavefronts drawn across it, strikes the boundary between two materials whose refractive indices you set. It splits into a reflected beam at the mirror angle and a refracted beam that changes speed, bunches or spreads its wavefronts and bends; push past the critical angle and the refracted beam vanishes.

members.dotPoint: Conduct a practical investigation to model how waves diffract through openings and around obstacles of different sizes
members.title: Ripple tank: waves bending round gaps
members.exam: A common mistake is drawing the waves after the gap with a shorter or longer wavelength, or saying they slow down. Only their direction changes. Draw the crests beyond the gap with the same spacing as before, and explain the amount of spreading by comparing the gap or obstacle size with the wavelength.
members.summary: A ripple tank seen from above. Straight waves from a paddle meet a barrier with a gap, or a single block; drag the slider to resize it and watch the waves fan out into semicircles near one wavelength, or pass almost straight through when it is many wavelengths wide.

members.dotPoint: Demonstrate the formation of a standing wave
members.title: Standing waves on a string
members.exam: The classic slip is saying adjacent nodes are one wavelength apart: they are half a wavelength apart, so each loop is λ/2. Count the loops to get n, use λ = 2L/n, then f = v/λ. Changing the harmonic changes f and λ, not the wave speed, which is set by the string.
members.summary: A string clamped at both ends vibrates in slow motion: a wave going right (gold) and its inverted reflection (white) slide through each other while their blue sum grows and shrinks in place, with nodes, antinodes and the wavelength marked as the harmonic slider fits one to six loops.

members.dotPoint: Explain the frequency shift phenomenon for sound waves and light waves (blueshift and redshift), as a source moves towards and away from an observer

members.exam: Common slips: mixing up the signs (both speeds are positive when moving towards each other, so a receding source makes the denominator v + v_source), or saying the wave travels faster ahead of the source. members.summary: A source glides right through still air, sending out circular wavefronts that bunch up ahead and stretch out behind, while observer A (ahead) and observer B (behind) flash on each arrival and trace the wave they receive. Sliders set the source and observer speeds with the formula worked live; the light toggle colours the wavefronts to show blueshift ahead and redshift behind.

members.dotPoint: solution concentration as a measure of the quantity of solute dissolved in a given mass or volume of solution (mol L-1, g L-1, %(m/v), %(v/v), ppm), including unit conversions
members.title: Concentration and dilution

members.dotPoint: the use of solubility tables and solubility graphs to predict experimental determination of ionic compound solubility; the effect of temperature on the solubility of a given solid, liquid or gas in water
members.title: Solubility changing with temperature
members.exam: Common slips: reading the curve at the wrong temperature, forgetting it is per 100 g of water so not scaling for 50 g, and saying gases dissolve more when hot. members.title: Dispersion of white light in a prism
members.exam: Students often say the prism adds colour, or that red bends most. For a rainbow, name all three steps: refraction in, reflection off the back, refraction out.
members.summary: A white beam passes through a flint-glass prism, a convex lens or a raindrop and fans into coloured rays, red bent least and violet most. Drag the slider to change the angle of incidence, the curvature of the lens or where sunlight strikes the drop.

Marks come from naming the mechanism: warm fluid rises because it is less dense, an object has thermal energy, and heat is the transfer. members.summary: A box of particles whose jiggle speed is the temperature. Switch between conduction along a solid bar, convection currents above a heater, radiation crossing a vacuum gap, and evaporation, where the fastest particles leave and the liquid left behind cools below the air around it.

The mass slider stretches or squeezes every stage.

members.exam: Common slip: measuring amplitude from crest to trough (that is twice the amplitude) or saying the rope moves along with the wave. Marks come from naming the particle motion relative to the energy direction, rearranging v = fλ and f = 1/T correctly, and converting units such as ms to s and cm to m.
members.summary: A rope wave and a spring wave run side by side across a 3 m strip, each with one amber tracked particle that only bobs up and down or slides back and forth. Sliders for wave speed, frequency and amplitude stretch or crowd the waves while the wavelength and period update live.

It splits into a reflected beam at the mirror angle and a refracted beam that changes speed, bunches or spreads its wavefronts and bends; push past the critical angle and the refracted beam vanishes.

runnersUp.dotPoint: describe how an increase in temperature corresponds to an increase in thermal energy (kinetic and potential energy of the atoms) of a system:

runnersUp.summary: A box of particles whose jiggle speed is the temperature. runnersUp.dotPoint: investigate and analyse theoretically and practically the energy required to:
runnersUp.title: Heating curve and latent heat

members.dotPoint: investigate and apply theoretically and practically concepts of current, resistance, potential difference (voltage drop) and power to the operation of electronic circuits comprising resistors, light bulbs, diodes, thermistors, light dependent resistors (LDRs), light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and potentiometers (quantitative analysis restricted to use of I=VR and P = VI)
members.title: I-V curves of non-ohmic devices
members.exam: Students often take resistance from the gradient of a curved I-V graph, or forget why a thermistor or LDR is non-ohmic. Held at one temperature or light level, its line is straight because R = V/I is constant; it is classed as non-ohmic because its resistance changes with temperature or light, including when its own current warms it. Resistance at a point is R = V/I using that point's coordinates. Marks come from naming the cause of the bend (filament heating, switch-on voltage, temperature or light), giving units, and using P = VI with values read off the graph.
members.summary: Pick a component and drag the voltage: its I-V curve traces out from the origin, an amber chord from the origin shows R = V/I at that point, and a small test circuit shows charge flowing at a rate set by the current. Temperature, light and knob sliders tilt the thermistor, LDR and potentiometer lines.

members.dotPoint: model household electricity connections as a simple DC circuit comprising fuses, switches, circuit breakers, loads and earth
members.title: Household circuit with fuses and earth
members.exam: Students often put the fuse or switch in the neutral, or say an RCD trips on an overload. Marks come from placing switches, fuses and breakers in the active, adding parallel currents with I = P/V to compare against the rating, and explaining an RCD by a difference between active and neutral currents, not by the size of the current.
members.summary: A 230 V supply feeds a lamp, toaster, heater and kettle in parallel on active, neutral and earth wires. Switch appliances on, add a fault in the toaster and choose a fuse, circuit breaker or RCD to watch the charge flow, the device melt or trip, or a person get a shock.

members.dotPoint: apply concepts of charge (Q), electric current (I), potential difference (V), energy (E) and power (P), in electric circuits
members.title: Current as flowing charge
members.exam: Students often draw conventional current the way the electrons move, or plug minutes and microcoulombs straight into I = q/t. Draw the arrow from + to − outside the cell, convert to coulombs and seconds first (2 min = 120 s), and give the answer in amperes.
members.summary: Free electrons drift through a metal wire between two terminals and a dashed gate counts the charge crossing it each second, which equals the current; the conventional current arrow points the other way, and switching to AC makes the drift and both arrows swing back and forth.

members.dotPoint: model resistance in series and parallel circuits using:
members.title: Ohm's law and resistance
members.exam: Students often call the gradient of an I–V graph the resistance. With I on the vertical axis the gradient is 1/R, and for a non-ohmic device R = V/I at that point, not the tangent slope. Put the ammeter in series and the voltmeter in parallel, and say a metal wire is ohmic only at constant temperature.
members.summary: Electrons drift through a lattice of vibrating ions in a wire wired to a cell, while the I–V graph traces out as you raise the voltage. Change the material, length, diameter or temperature and the straight line tilts; switch to a filament globe and the line bends into a curve.

members.dotPoint: investigate and analyse theoretically and practically electric circuits using the relationships: I=Qt, V=EQ, P=Et=VI
members.title: Electrical power and energy in circuits
members.exam: Students often treat voltage as energy rather than energy per coulomb, or forget to convert minutes to seconds in ΔE = PΔt. Write the chain I = Q/t, V = E/Q, P = VI = ΔE/Δt, keep SI units (J, C, s, W), and name what the energy becomes (light, heat) when asked about transformations.
members.summary: Charges circle a battery-and-globe loop carrying gold energy halos that shrink to nothing in the globe; dragging the voltage makes the halos bigger, the charges faster, the globe brighter and the P = VI rectangle grow in both directions at once.

members.dotPoint: justify the use of selected meters (ammeter, voltmeter, multimeter) in circuits
members.title: Series and parallel circuits
members.exam: Common slips: putting a voltmeter in series, saying current is used up by the first resistor, or forgetting to flip 1/R at the end. members.dotPoint: describe the properties of α, β-, β+ and γ radiation
members.title: Alpha, beta and gamma decay
members.exam: Students often balance only the mass numbers, write a beta particle as ⁰₁e, or forget to change the element symbol. Marks come from showing A and Z both balancing, writing β− as ⁰₋₁e and β+ as ⁰₊₁e, and naming the daughter from its new atomic number.
members.summary: A nucleus fires an alpha particle, a beta-minus electron, a beta-plus positron or a gamma photon at paper, aluminium and lead. The nuclear equation above it fills in the daughter element as the mass and atomic numbers balance, and each emission stops where its penetrating power runs out.

members.dotPoint: analyse decay series diagrams with reference to type of decay and stability of isotopes
members.title: Decay series and the band of stability
members.exam: Students mix up arrow directions or assume the axes, and count only alphas so the atomic numbers do not balance. Marks come from reading the axes first, naming each step as alpha or beta from its change in N and Z, and checking the total: the A drop over 4 gives the alphas, and the Z change then fixes the number of betas.
members.summary: An N-Z chart with the whole band of stability on the left and a zoomed grid on the right. Each tap adds one decay arrow, alpha two squares down-left and beta-minus one square up-left, until uranium-238 or thorium-232 lands on stable lead, or two light nuclides beta-decay into the band from either side.

members.dotPoint: explain the effects of α, β and γ radiation on humans, including:
members.title: Radiation dose: grey, sievert and the body
members.exam: Students often multiply by the tissue weighting factor before the radiation weighting factor, or label absorbed dose in sievert. Marks come from showing D = E ÷ m with mass in kilograms and units of Gy, then H = D × wR in Sv, then effective dose = H × wT in Sv, with units on every line.
members.summary: A torso with an alpha, beta or gamma source outside the body or inhaled into the lungs, drawing each radiation's track and ionisations. Beside it, three bars on a log scale turn the energy the lungs absorb into absorbed dose in grey, then equivalent and effective dose in sievert.

members.dotPoint: analyse, graphically, non-uniform motion in a straight line
members.title: Motion graphs of a journey
members.exam: Students often read the height of a v–t graph as displacement, or count area below the axis as positive. Marks go to taking the gradient from a tangent on a curved s–t graph (not s ÷ t at one point), giving units (m/s, m/s²), and treating area below the axis as negative displacement.
members.summary: One object travels a straight track while its displacement–time, velocity–time and acceleration–time graphs draw themselves in step. Switch between the gradient bridge (tangent lines) and the area bridge (shaded areas) to see how each graph builds the next, for a road trip, a ball thrown up and a dropped ball.

members.dotPoint: analyse rate of energy transfer using power: P=Et
members.title: Power and efficiency of energy transfer
members.exam: Students often think a more powerful motor uses less energy, forget to convert kJ, kW or minutes into J, W and s, or flip the efficiency fraction and get more than 100%. Marks come from writing P = E/t or η = useful out ÷ total in, substituting with units, and checking η sits between 0 and 1.
members.summary: A motor winds a 20 kg crate up 5 m while an energy against time graph traces energy in and useful energy out, their slopes being the two powers, with the gap between them shaded as wasted heat and a stacked bar showing the efficiency.

members.dotPoint: apply concepts of momentum to linear motion: p = mv
members.title: Collision lab: momentum before and after
members.exam: Students often drop the minus sign when a cart rebounds, so the totals do not match, or claim kinetic energy is conserved in every collision. Marks come from setting a positive direction, writing m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ with signs, and explaining differences in real data with friction and measurement uncertainty.
members.summary: Cart A rolls into cart B on a track while ticker-tape dots record both speeds. Load cart B or change the bumper and the carts bounce, split or stick, yet the momentum arrows after the crash always add tip to tail to the same total as before.
